points.title: Les pronoms sujets et le verbe avoir au présent
points.explanationEn:
French has eight subject pronouns where English has seven, and mapping them correctly is the first real hurdle: je (I), tu (you, informal singular), il (he/it, masculine), elle (she/it, feminine), on (one/we/people, informal), nous (we), vous (you, formal or plural), ils (they, masculine or mixed group), elles (they, all-feminine group). Two things trip up English speakers immediately. First, il and elle are used not just for people but for objects and ideas too, because every French noun has a grammatical gender — 'le livre' (the book) is 'il', 'la table' (the table) is 'elle'. Second, for a group made of any mix of masculine and feminine (even 99 women and 1 man), French defaults to the masculine plural 'ils'. This is a grammatical convention, not a statement about the group.

Avoir ('to have') is, like être, a highly irregular verb that must be memorized as a full set: j'ai, tu as, il/elle/on a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. Note the elision: je becomes j' before a vowel sound (j'ai, not 'je ai'). This elision rule is not optional stylistic choice — it is required whenever je (and several other short words like le, la, ce, ne) precedes a word starting with a vowel or a mute h.

Avoir is used far more broadly in French than 'to have' is in English. Many expressions that use 'to be' in English use avoir in French — famously, age ('J'ai vingt ans' = literally 'I have twenty years' = 'I am twenty years old'), and also sensations like hunger, thirst, fear, and being hot or cold (avoir faim, avoir soif, avoir peur, avoir chaud, avoir froid). English speakers who translate word-for-word will say 'Je suis vingt ans' or 'Je suis faim', which are both wrong — you must reach for avoir instead of être in these fixed expressions.

examples.fr: J'ai un frère et une sœur.
examples.en: I have a brother and a sister.
examples.note: 'Je' elides to "j'" before the vowel sound of 'ai'.
Literally 'you have what age' — avoir, not être, expresses age.

examples.fr: Ils ont un chien et un chat.
examples.en: They have a dog and a cat.
examples.note: Mixed or all-masculine group of nouns → 'ils'.

examples.en: They (all female) have an appointment at noon.

examples.note: Literally 'I have hunger and I have thirst' — avoir expresses physical states, not être.
'On' takes the same verb form as il/elle: 'a', not 'ai' or 'avons'.

commonMistakes: Saying 'Je suis vingt ans' or 'Je suis faim' by translating English 'to be' word-for-word instead of using avoir for age and physical sensations.
Forgetting the elision and writing/saying 'je ai' instead of "j'ai".
Using 'ils' vs 'elles' based on which gender feels more numerous or important in a group, rather than the rule that any mixed-gender group defaults to 'ils'.
Conjugating 'on' with the wrong ending (e.g. 'on avons') instead of treating it as a third-person-singular pronoun that always takes the il/elle verb form ('on a').
Applying 'il/elle' only to people and using 'it' as a mental placeholder for objects, then getting stuck because French has no separate word for 'it'.
whyItTrips: English has no grammatical gender for objects, so the idea that 'the table' is inherently 'elle' feels arbitrary and has no equivalent instinct to draw on.
English uses 'to be' for age and physical sensations ('I am hungry', 'I am 20'), so reaching for 'to have' in French requires overriding a deeply automatic English pattern.
English 'they' is gender-neutral for groups, so French forcing a masculine default ('ils') for mixed groups feels unfamiliar and easy to get backwards.
